sentences.text: Australovenator was a large predator approximately 6 meters long, with a body mass ranging from 310 to 500 kilograms.
Although no skull has been found, the animal likely possessed an elongated, slender head similar to other megaraptorans.
Its lower jaws were lightly constructed and held 19 teeth in each side.
The dinosaur featured massive forelimbs with bowed, S-shaped upper arm bones that ended in giant, sharp claws.
This giant, recurved hand claw is a defining trait of the megaraptoran clade.
The holotype specimen, which serves as the basis for the species description, was discovered near Elderslie Station in 2006.
Scott Hocknull and colleagues formally described Australovenator in 2009.
This description was published in the journal PLOS One later that same year.
The specific name wintonensis was included in this 2009 publication by Hocknull et al.
The preserved material includes both lower jaws, numerous teeth, ribs, and bones from the arms, legs, and feet.
Australovenator belongs to the clade Megaraptora, a group that existed during the Cretaceous in Asia, South America, and Oceania.
The name Megaraptora was coined in 2010 by paleontologist Roger Benson and colleagues.
A 2025 analysis by Ibiricu and colleagues classified Australovenator as a basal member of Megaraptoridae.
Despite these findings, the higher-level classification relationships of the group Megaraptora remain uncertain.
Australovenator lived during the early Late Cretaceous, roughly 95 million years ago, in what is now Australia.
The rock layers containing the fossil date to the Cenomanian stage.
Sandstone from the Winton Formation indicates an environment dominated by oxbow lakes or similar lacustrine settings.
However, the holotype was recovered from the lower part of the Winton Formation, which is dated to the late Albian.
Scientists debate whether Megaraptora, including Australovenator, are carcharodontosaurs, basal coelurosaurs, or tyrannosauroids.
A 2016 study suggested Australovenator could be an allosauroid or a basal coelurosaur.
Conversely, a recent phylogenetic analysis suggests Australovenator is a tyrannosauroid, similar to all other megaraptorids.
Some researchers have proposed that Rapator might be the closest relative, or sister taxon, of Australovenator.
It is debated whether Rapator and Australovenator are the same species, with some arguing they are distinct due to age and morphological differences.

Additionally, a specimen from the Winton Formation shows differences from Australovenator, leading to debates about whether it represents a different species, age-related changes, or individual variation.
